items.title: Adiós a Jean-François Leroy, apasionado director de Visa pour l’Image y defensor del fotoperiodismo
items.excerpt: Jean-François Leroy © Stephan Vanfleteren Director of the Visa pour l’Image festival of photojournalism for nearly 40 years, Jean-François Leroy passed away just as it opened for the 38th time Jean-François Leroy, co-founder and director of Visa pour l’Image, has died.
items.content:
Jean-François Leroy © Stephan Vanfleteren

Director de la Visa para l’Image festival de fotoperiodismo durante casi 40 años, Jean-François Leroy falleció tal como se abrió por 38a vez

Jean-François Leroy, cofundador y director de Visa pour l’Image, ha muerto. Leroy falleció de cáncer el 31 de agosto, así como el festival de fotoperiodismo con el que fue abierto sinónimo para su 38a edición.

Nacido en París en 1956, Leroy trabajó como fotógrafo para Sipa Press y editor en jefe de Photo Magazine; Se convirtió en director de Visa en 1989, cuando se fundó. Bajo su reloj el festival se convirtió en un evento celebrado y un lugar de encuentro clave, con colectivos respetados como VII y Noor eligiendo lanzar en la semana de apertura de Visa (VII en 2001 y Noor en 2007). Conocido por su pasión por la fotografía documental, Leroy fue galardonado con un Chevalier des Arts et Lettres y un Chevalier de l’Ordre du Mérite francés.

“Es algo trágico, Jean-François saliendo de este mundo, y se puede ver que hay una merecida efusión [de homenajes]”, dice Jillian Edelstein, quien ganó la Visa d’Or en 1997 por su trabajo en la Comisión de la Verdad y la Reconciliación de Sudáfrica. “Visa ha respaldado y apoyado a tantos fotoperiodistas y, dado qué tipo de mundo estamos en, eso es tan importante.

“Jean-François tuvo un buen ojo, y habit al festival a existir y a tener éxito”, dice Kadir van Lohuizen, un fotógrafo documental y cofundador de Noor, que fue galardonado con la Visa d’Or en 2007 por su trabajo en Chad. “La gente ha declarado Visa muerta muchas veces, pero Jean-François fue una especie de camaleón y siempre fue de encontrar otro apoyo”.

“Durante los casi 40 años que hemos estado haciendo Visa pour l’Image en Perpignan, sólo ha habido una regla: exhibir y proyectar lo que creemos que es lo mejor en el fotoperiodismo”. Jean-François Leroy

Celebrada en Perpignan, al sur de Francia, las exposiciones y eventos de Visa tienen lugar en lugares históricos como el Couvent des Minimes, un antiguo convento del siglo XV, y el Campo Santo, un gran claustro al aire libre; respaldado por Canon desde 1990, cuando tuvo lugar el primer festival, es libre de asistir. La edición de este año, programada por Leroy, incluye exposiciones como Hashem conflicto de Abdulsa

Visa está financiada en parte por dinero público y el gobierno local de Perpignan ha sido la extrema derecha Rassemblement National desde 2020; en marzo de 2026, el Louis Aliot de RN fue reelegido como alcalde. El RN ha cortado el apoyo a los cuerpos culturales locales, pero el festival ha sufrido. ”Él [Aliot] podría haber arruinado el festival cuando asumió el cargo; él no, y él sigue ejerciendo presión Libération en 2023. “Así que hablamos de ‘una neutralidad benevolente’”.

El artículo de Libération fue impulsado por una exposición de Jordi Borràs a la extrema derecha en Europa en esa edición del festival, que el fotógrafo afirmó que fue censurado; su presentación original incluía imágenes de Marine Le Pen [líder de la RN] que fueron removidas sin su conocimiento antes de que se inaugurara su exposición. La respuesta de Leroy fue robusta, informó Libération“En general, su historia fue investigada muy a fondo, pero en el medio, había tres fotos de mierda de 2017 – una de Marine Le Pen en un podio, una de una multitud, y uno de un tipo que llevaba una bufanda – que parecía que habían sido arrancados en una prisa y debilitado toda la pieza.

“Los removimos durante la edición, junto con otros, manteniendo 50 de 72. Esto ocurriría sin que los fotógrafos sean notificados, dado el volumen de historias que manejamos y la relación de confianza que hemos construido con la comunidad durante tanto tiempo”.

De hecho, la de pasión de Leroy por la fotografía documental fue criticada a veces por ser poco convincente; cuando Visa se enfrentaba a censura este año, por la falta de trabajo de mujeres fotógrafos, Leroy defendió firmemente su posición. “Durante los casi 40 años que hemos estado haciendo Visa pour l’Image en Perpignan, sólo ha una regla: exhibir y revisar lo que creemos que era el mejor en el periodismo de julio

“Sin embargo, a medida que nos acercamos a la apertura de nuestra 38a edición, hemos notado que ha habido una disminución significativa en el número de presentaciones al festival de mujeres; una caída que viene en un momento en que ha habido una disminución general de la producción debido a recortes en los presupuestos para la fotografía en los medios de comunicación.

“Este año, las mujeres representan sólo el 22% del programa de festivales (exhibiciones y proyecciones). Nos gustaría que esta figura fuera más alta, como ha sido el caso en ediciones anteriores. Pero los fotoperiodistas femeninas, jóvenes y establecidos, a menudo nos han dicho que no quieren ser seleccionados o ganar premios basados en la discriminación positiva. Más bien, les gustaría ser reconocidos basados en la fuerza de su talento.”

Leroy explica que Visa apoya a las mujeres fotoperiodistas con iniciativas como el Canon Female Photojournalist Grant y el Françoise Demulder Photography Grants, y que el porcentaje de mujeres fotógrafas en el festival reflejaba el número de presentaciones de mujeres. Pero su declaración se reunió con resistencia.

Más ampliamente, tal vez, el reto ahora es cómo evolucionar Visa pour l’Image, cuando las comisiones editoriales han disminuido, y AI, noticias falsas y regímenes autoritarios han apilado presión sobre la fotografía documental. “Ruth Eichhorn [director de fotografía de GEO Magazine] pasó el mismo día que Jean-François, y se siente como el final de una era”, dice Van Lohuizen más que nunca.

“Pero sabes, Jean-François no habría podido dirigir el festival tan exitosamente durante tantos años sin su equipo, y especialmente Delphine [Delphine Lelu, director ejecutivo]. Debe ser representativo para todos ellos, pero espero que el festival sobreviva, y que la filosofía detrás del festival sobreviva”.

Las exposiciones en Visa pour l’Image están abiertas hasta el 13 de septiembre en Perpignan, al sur de Francia, y pueden visitarse en https://visapourlimage.com/en/

El puesto Farewell Jean-François Leroy, passionate director of Visa pour l’Image and defender of photojournalism apareció primero. 1854 Photography.

items.title: Haciendo el North de Chris Killip
items.excerpt: Seacoal beach, Lynemouth, Northumberland, 1983 © Thames & Hudson / Chris Killip Photography Trust / Magnum Photos “To be given the keys to the archive is a privilege,” says Mark Holborn who, nearly four decades after editing Chris Killip’s seminal In Flagrante, was truste
items.content:
Playa de Seacoal, Lynemouth, Northumberland, 1983 © Támesis & Hudson / Chris Killip Photography Trust / Magnum Fotos

“Se les dará las llaves del archivo es un privilegio”, dice Mark Holborn quien, casi cuatro décadas después de editar la seminal de Chris Killip En Flagrante, fue confiado por el hijo de Killip Matthew para hacer un nuevo libro de su trabajo, Norte

Cuando Mark Holborn se sentó con una copia terminada Norte, el libro que editó del archivo de Chris Killip, se sorprendió. “Ayer recibí una enorme carga del libro cuando lo miré”, dice. “Es casi visceral para mí”.

Había visto pruebas y archivos PDF a lo largo de su producción, pero esta fue la primera vez que había girado las páginas del libro físico antes. “Es como tocar un álbum por primera vez. Te sientas y te vas de principio a fin”.

Hay más en juego aquí que la finalización de otro fotolibro. Holborn primero trabajó con Killip hace casi cuatro décadas en In Flagrante, que fue publicado por Secker & Warburg en 1988 y ahora es considerado como uno de los fotolibros de la era post-industrial británica. Killip murió en 2020, por lo que fue su hijo, Matthew, quien dio a Holborn pleno acceso al archivo, incluyendo fotografías que el editor nunca había visto, junto con las que ha conocido por la mayor parte de su vida adulta.

“Para este, tengo una especie de deber”, Holborn me dice en una videollamada. “Killip no está aquí. Ser dado las llaves del archivo es un falso, que tengo que calificar. Quiero hacerle justicia. Esto no se trata de la proyección de mi propia fantasía del Norte. Se trata de mi lealtad a él.”

“Lo primero que se ve en las fotografías es que son notablemente elegantes. Su elegancia está casi en contraste con su tema.” Mark Holborn

Norte, publicado por Thames & Hudson, no es ni una retrospectiva convencional ni una colección de los mayores éxitos de Killip. Incluye 224 fotografías, muchas anteriormente inéditas, sigue una secuencia extendida.

También viene menos de cuatro años después de la editorial Chris Killip 1946–2020, que se concibió en conjunción con una exposición internacional de giras y organizada alrededor de la amplitud de los proyectos individuales de Killip. Holborn dice que el libro, que proporciona un relato definitivo de la vida y el trabajo del fotógrafo, “ servirá a los historiadores bien en el futuro”. Pero su propio principio editorial es casi su inverso.

“Está tratando de encontrar una estructura que pudiera contener una sola narrativa fluida”, dice, “porque eso es lo que me interesa y esa es la forma en que trabajo”.

Los límites del proyecto se disuelven en consecuencia. Seacoal, Skinningrove, Huddersfield y las fotografías hechas a través del principio se encuentran dentro del mismo flujo, mientras que el cuerpo principal de trabajo se enmarca inesperadamente por fotografías antiguas de la isla natal de Killip del Hombre, y imágenes posteriores de peregrinaciones en Croagh Patrick y Máméan en Irlanda – lo que Holborn llama “os de piedras o fronteras dentro”.

Malas tarros de edición, a menudo imperceptible, mientras que la buena edición casi no se da cuenta. Norte nos lleva de vuelta en el tiempo para ver no sólo lo que vio Killip, sino lo que discernió. El efecto es una especie de sentido mágico. La astuta comprensión de Holborn de la obra de Killip, junto con la magia que trae para juntar imágenes – pares trabajando en armonía, estableciendo una secuencia para lograr una coherencia poética – nos permite ser completamente absorbidos dentro del ojo de la mente del fotógrafo.

Muchos queridos son asesinados a lo largo del camino. Las imágenes individuales dan paso al todo. Norte nunca mejora la dignidad concisa y enojada de In Flagrante, utiliza sus 300 páginas para transmitir la lenta determinación de Killip de mapear los márgenes – entre ciudad y país, el mar y tierra, el pasado industrial y el futuro incierto – y su conexión con la gente atrapada en el medio.

La secuencia también trae terreno a la vanguardia. Killip se celebra por la intensidad de sus encuentros con personas – niños y adolescentes, trabajadores astilleros, comunidades pesqueras, familias que recogen carbón de mar de la playa de Lynemouth – pero Norte deja más clara la continuidad del paisaje que les rodea. Calles y viviendas, playas, astilleros y estructuras industriales deja de ser fondos; la gente y el lugar se convierten en parte de la misma descripción histórica.

Holborn evitó deliberadamente muchas de las fotos más conocidas de Killip. “Estaba persiguiendo algo más, algo totalmente diferente”, dice. “No quería que este libro pareciera algo que habías visto antes.” Sólo tres fotografías de In Flagrante “La inclusión de esas tres imágenes fue una gran concesión por mi parte a lo que había llegado antes”. Uno, la famosa imagen de Killip de un niño en una pared en Jarrow, se convierte en “un coda de tipos”. Norte, “tanto la continuidad como la salida”

Tales decisiones ponen énfasis inusual en el editor, un papel que Holborn ha ocupado durante más de cuatro décadas, pero que, cuando In Flagrante fue hecho, todavía no estaba claramente definido. Comenzó en Cámara creativa antes de mudarse a Nueva York a principios de los años 80 para trabajar en Aperture, una experiencia que lo sumergió en una cultura fotográfica que operaba a una escala diferente a Gran Bretaña. Su carrera posterior ha abarcado largas colaboraciones con Don McCullin y Daido Moriyama; grandes proyectos que involucraban los archivos de Larry Burrows, Lenart Nilsson y NASA; y libros con artistas como Lucian Freud.

Lo más importante para la historia de Killip, en Aperture ayudó a traer Nan Goldin La balada de dependencia sexual "Nan era crudo, auténtico, y por lo tanto me parecía totalmente obvio publicar La balada de dependencia sexualAgrega que trabajar con Killip parecía igualmente obvio.

El sentimiento era mutuo. Cuando David Godwin en Secker & Warburg ofreció a Killip la oportunidad de hacer un libro – después de su exposición de 1985 con Graham Smith, Otro país en la Serpentine – Killip pidió específicamente a Holborn como editor. Más tarde recordó que la experiencia de Holborn en Aperture, y su exposición a la mejor fotografía contemporánea que se publica internacionalmente, ofreció algo que se sentía alejado, viviendo en Newcastle.

Aperture “fue un lugar muy bueno para servir a un aprendiz”, dice Hoborn. “Podría traer eso de vuelta, en cierto sentido, que es una de las razones por las que comenzó a trabajar con Killip. Creo que fue usado por algún sentido del internacionalismo que podría haber traído conmigo”.

Holborn ya había probado algunas de las ideas que formarían In Flagrante. En 1986 publicó fotografías de Killip Seacoal en Aperture revista, que los atraviesa por el canal y les da la máxima altura. “Me encantó el impacto de la escala”, recuerda.

Para In Flagrante, Killip llegó a la casa de Holborn en Londres con impresiones de trabajo y un tonto preliminar. Abandonaron el maniquí y comenzaron de nuevo, poniendo las fotos en el piso; Holborn posteriormente construyó otro muñeco en su mesa de cocina usando impresiones, cartas y cintas. Su descripción de sus respectivos roles es desarmadamente simple: “Él era un artista. Él hizo fotos. Yo los absorbí y los arreglé.”

“Arreglado” subestima la intervención. El formato vertical fue la decisión de Holborn; él resistió un gran libro horizontal porque temía que se asemejaría a una “portafolio refinada” (como Steidl haría casi 30 años después con En Flagrante Dos), en contraste abrupto con las fotografías mismas. En lugar de eso, las imágenes corrieron frecuentemente a través de la barra.

“Un portafolio de buenas imágenes no tiene el voltaje correcto”, dice Holborn. “Este es un libro enojado. Es salvaje”. Un contemporáneo Hora de salir La revisión se quejó de que el truco se ejecuta a través de las fotografías de Killip. Holborn sigue sin disculparse: “Bueno, por supuesto que lo hicimos. Eso fue muy propósito. Se beneficia de la escala, y el canalla sirve. Es un ataque; un asalto a las imágenes mismas. Sin ella, el libro sería dócil.”

Para Holborn, la edición de un libro fotográfico está más cerca de la edición de la película que de la organización de un portafolio. Una secuencia debe convertirse en “cumulativa emocionalmente”, controlando la experiencia del lector del tiempo, dados. “Te mueve rápido, y pausas, y te desaceleras, y aceleras... La mirada al libro tiene su propio tiempo”.

Cuatro décadas después, lo que Holborn ve en las imágenes individuales de Killip es una tensión similar entre la forma y el contenido. “Lo primero que ves en las fotografías es que son notablemente elegantes”, dice. “Su elegancia está casi en contraste con su tema”.

Las fotografías de Killip lentamente medidas, controladas formalmente poseen lo que Holborn describe en Norte como una “gracia pictórica”, a veces tan pronunciada que casi contradice la realidad estelar que se está representando. Sin embargo, lo que golpea a Holborn es igualmente su ternura. “Es un mundo muy brutal, y dentro de este mundo brutal hay escenas notables de ternura”, señala. Los niños son sostenidos y abrazados; los perros y cachorros son manejados cariñosamente; los caballos en la playa del mar hay más que las bestias de carga.

Que la humanidad complica el conocido cortocircuito de Killip como fotógrafo de la Gran Bretaña de Thatcher. Norte Comenzar en 1975 y fueron hechos por los gobiernos obreros y conservadores por igual; reducirlos a la oposición al poder conservador, escribe Holborn, es “muy simplista”. Lo que Killip estaba presenciando fue una transformación histórica más grande y fundamental.

“Estaba fotografiando un mundo que pasaba mientras lo fotografiaba”, dice Holborn. “Era un mundo en transición, y el viejo mundo estaba decayendo y colapsando por todos lados”. La diferencia es que Killip y el público original para In Flagrante todavía vivían dentro de esa transición. “En el momento en que Killip lo estaba haciendo, lo sintió, pero todavía estaba allí”, dice Holborn. “Ahora se ha ido”.

Por lo tanto, el tiempo ha alterado las imágenes tanto como tiene los lugares que describen. Holborn se dio cuenta mientras trabajaba en Norte que la distancia que separa a un joven lector hoy del noreste de Killip es aproximadamente equivalente a la que separa los años 80 de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Las fotografías que una vez describieron un presente desplegable se han convertido en evidencia histórica, y algunos han pasado de la historia fotográfica a la memoria colectiva; "Cuando alguien quiere encontrar imágenes del norte de Inglaterra a finales del siglo XX, se convertirán en Killip."

Norte es un intento de familiarizar ese cuerpo familiar de trabajo – para volver al archivo, eliminar muchas de las imágenes a través de las cuales Killip ha llegado a ser conocido, y construir otra ruta a través del paisaje que fotografió. Holborn describe la relación entre fotógrafo y editor como un proceso de “osmosis”, en el que cada uno absorbe gradualmente la sensibilidad del otro. Con Killip ya no está presente para aprobar o rechazar sus opciones, esa relación ahora depende de algo más elus.

“He hecho una vida con mis ojos”, dice Holborn. “Cómo mirar es cómo ganó mi vida durante los últimos 40 o 50 años. Tengo que confiar en eso.”

Chris Killip: El norte es editado por Mark Holborn y publicado por Thames & Hudson, precio £75 www.thamesandhudson.com

items.title: En el foco: Takuma Nakahira
items.excerpt: Takuma Nakahira in the coffee shop at the Nagisa Hotel in Zushi, Japan, February 1972, from At the Limits of the Gaze: Selected Writings by Takuma Nakahira (Aperture, 2025) © The Estate of Isao Sekiguchii Takuma Nakahira was a prolific theorist as well as a cutting-edge image
items.content:
Takuma Nakahira en la cafetería del Hotel Nagisa en Zushi, Japón, Febrero de 1972, de En los Límites de la Gaze: Escrituras seleccionadas por Takuma Nakahira (Apertura, 2025) © La finca de Isao Sekiguchii

Takuma Nakahira era un teorista prolífico, así como un creador de imágenes de vanguardia y cofundador del radical Provoke Ahora, por primera vez, sus ensayos clave de 1970 se han traducido al inglés

Takuma Nakahira no es famosa en Occidente, y en Japón es quizás más conocido como fotógrafo. Pero el cofundador del legendario Provoke La revista también fue un crítico prolífico y ensayista, explorando el medio de la fotografía en artículos en revistas de arte y revistas literarias que finalmente fueron recogidos en libros. Ahora una selección de sus ensayos se ha publicado por primera vez en inglés, editado y traducido por expertos en fotografía japonesa Daniel Abbe y Franz Prichard. A los Límites de la Gaze recopila 10 textos publicados entre 1970 y 75, que van desde el jazz hasta Eugène Atget a los medios de comunicación, y muestran a Nakahira como radical, cosmopolita y todavía muy relevante.

“Nakahira consideró lo que significa ser ‘contemporario’, la idea de que personas como Walter Benjamin iterado ciertas ideas mucho antes en la historia de la modernidad”, dice Prichard. “Siendo un izquierdista, Nakahira era firme que las condiciones materiales no habían cambiado realmente entre su tiempo y ese momento anterior; él llamó la atención a esta. Y la potencia política de su cuestionamiento y el interrogatorio de la continuidad

“La potencia política del cuestionamiento y el interrogatorio del poder de Nakahira ante los medios visuales sólo se ha amplificado con el tiempo” – Franz Prichard

Como señala Prichard, la aproximación de Nakahira a la fotografía era inseparable de su política. Provoke fue fundada en 1968 en medio de protestas en Japón, Francia, Checoslovaquia y más allá, y cuestionaron imágenes como parte de un interrogatorio más amplio de cómo nos relacionamos con el mundo; Nakahira publicó un fotolibro en 1970 titulado Para un idioma que venga. La revista y libro rechazan caminos fáciles de la fotografía al conocimiento, y abandonan el documental directo a favor de imágenes más allá de la legibilidad, pero más cerca de la experiencia vivida. Ambos cuestionan también la estructura de poder incrustada en la cámara como escribió Nakahira en su ensayo de 1972 La Ilusión Documento Llamado: De Documento a Monumento: “...Contra nuestra asociación inmediata del documento de la palabra con un punto de vista objetivo, impersonal, quería repensar esta palabra a través de un énfasis sólo en el encuentro sin fin entre el mundo y el yo.”

En su ensayo de 1975 La voluntad hacia la historia: el poder potencial del surrealismo, Nakahira escribe que el surrealismo fue un intento de liberación total del humano, mientras tanto, y argumenta, “por eso fue el primer tiro disparado contra la lógica del positivismo, que apoya el sistema moderno del capital”. ¿Por qué una Guía Botánica Ilustrada? argumenta en líneas similares, enfatizando la subjetividad y el diálogo sobre la autoridad insensible y central. “La mirada no puede suceder aparte del cuerpo”, escribe, agregando, “Por mucho que pueda mirar al mundo, siempre me devolverá la mirada de las cosas al mismo tiempo”.

Pero la posición de Nakahira también cambió con el tiempo, Abbe y Prichard señalan; se desilusionó con el nuevo lenguaje fotográfico que él y Provoke había tratado de construir después de que fuera cooptado para la publicidad, y a mediados de los años 70 estaba escribiendo menos políticamente. También varió sus temas según la comisión de la revista, desde revistas de prensa vanguardistas a los más establecidos Cámara Asahi. A los Límites de la Gaze incluye ensayos de sus dos colecciones – ¿Por qué? Guía Botánica Ilustrada? Escribidos Coleccionados en Imágenes (1973) y Duel on Photography (1977, coautor de Kishin Shinoyama) – y por lo tanto “dos momentos discursivos en los que está coleccionando sus pensamientos de maneras muy diferentes, en contextos muy diferentes”, explica Prichard. Él y Abbe enfatizan que su libro traduce una fracción de la producción total de Nakahira también – sabían que a menudo servirá como una introducción, dice Abbe, aunque dejaron “como muchos consejos como sea posible a lo que hay más

Originalmente interesado en la poesía, Nakahira también experimentó con su escritura, a veces adoptando la postura impersonal de un ensayista convencional, en otras ocasiones un enfoque de primera persona, más diarista. Interlude narra apasionadamente quemar sus cuadernos y negativos, y beber con un extraño pasajero, refiriéndose a la quemadura del licor duro y su propia “conciencia cerrada”. “No tenía idea de lo que haría después de esto. Pero nunca volveré a tomar una fotografía, pensé. No puedo convertirme en un coleccionista de recuerdos, pensé”, escribe, después agregando, “No había límite entre el mar y el cielo, sólo la esfera celestial.

La escritura de Nakahira aquí es lírica, y este ensayo apunta a solaparse entre su escritura y fotografía; en otro lugar destaca las diferencias entre texto e imágenes, sin embargo, contrastando un documento visual de un árbol individual con el generalizado – o universal, o incluso objetivo – “árbol” convocado por la palabra, en su ensayo de 1970 ¿La fotografía ha sido capaz de provocar el lenguaje?. A veces la escritura de Nakahira informa a la fotografía y viceversa, notas de la Abadía, pero en general los vínculos directos son raros. “No están en pistas separadas como si nunca se intersectan, pero sólo están tocando flojamente”, sonríe.

Incluso así, Nakahira es una lectura clave para aquellos interesados en las imágenes y la cultura visual – o en la cartografía de perspectivas antiimperiales. Un crítico del papel de la posguerra de Estados Unidos en Japón, Nakahira también cuestionó la historia japonesa, y en particular el enfoque de la nación hacia las Islas Okinawa del Pacífico. “Viejos venden sus cosas sin pronunciar una palabra”, escribe en Mi reflejo de ojos desnudos: 1974, Okinawa, verano¿Qué dice el silencio de esos hombres y mujeres?

En los Límites de la Gaze: Escrituras seleccionadas por Takuma Nakahira, editado por Daniel Abbe y Franz Prichard, es publicado por Aperture, precio $30.

items.title: Rania Matar’s Where Do I Go? documents Lebanon’s women through a question the country won’t stop asking
items.excerpt: From Where Do I Go © Rania Matar Rania Matar returned to Lebanon for years to photograph the women navigating a country in perpetual crisis. By the time her book was published, war had returned with a question impossible to ignore The Holiday Inn Beirut has not been repaired
items.content:
From Where Do I Go © Rania Matar

Rania Matar returned to Lebanon for years to photograph the women navigating a country in perpetual crisis. By the time her book was published, war had returned with a question impossible to ignore

The Holiday Inn Beirut has not been repaired in 50 years. Back when it opened in 1974, it was a monument to the city’s glamour – a 28-floor tower of modernist optimism overlooking the Mediterranean. It was gutted in the first years of the Lebanese Civil War, when militias fought floor by floor for control of its height, using its rooftop as a sniper nest, burning it from the inside out. The Palestinian-Lebanese-American artist and photographer Rania Matar was living nearby, and remembers watching the ‘Battle of the Hotels’ from her apartment, as “every single room burned one by one.” 

Matar was a child when she watched the building die; half a century later she returned to photograph young women inside it, and this act is perhaps the quintessence of what Where Do I Go? لوين روح؟ is about. It took Matar “years” to get access to the former hotel, which is off-limits to the public and restricted under Lebanese Army control; even when she had permission to shoot, she had to climb a spiral staircase for 24 floors with her subject and two army escorts to do so.

Since the Civil War, a deadlock has kept the hotel frozen, its ownership split between a Lebanese company that wants to convert it into condominiums and a Kuwaiti group that wants to demolish it. Its heavily damaged carcass continues to pose the question: what do you do with a wound you cannot seem to close? But revisiting it to take photographs was “pretty exhilarating”, Matar says. “Exhilarating, healing, whatever you want.”

“If they’re replying, then they’re willing to be part of this, and I figure they’re interesting enough to be willing to put themselves out there.” Rania Matar

In psychology, the process of revisiting a charged experience to honour the feeling without being imprisoned by it is known as memory reconsolidation; for Matar, the project started organically after she visited Lebanon following the 2020 port explosion. Observing women working to reconstruct the city, she realised there was a wave of young people who wanted to leave the country, but unsure whether they should. “I saw myself in them,” she says. 

Matar left Lebanon in 1984, when she was 20; these women were the same age now. “My friends who didn’t leave, their kids are leaving. It feels like there’s a sense of history that keeps repeating itself,” she reflects. Over multiple visits, her approach stayed the same – put a call for subjects on Instagram, speak with whoever responded, and build a collaboration from there. 

“I don’t ask for pictures or anything [before meeting],” she says. “If they’re replying, then they’re willing to be part of this, and I figure they’re interesting enough to be willing to put themselves out there.”

Despite the age gap, collaboration bloomed between Matar and her subjects, and their shared memories of the same country. One woman led her to the south of Lebanon, to a gigantic bomb crater in the middle of a gorgeous landscape, and a scene built around sandbags. “I give them so much credit that they’re willing to do this,” Matar shares. 

“We went to this place, and she’s standing on these sandbags where snipers hid during the war. And she was wearing, by her own choice, her mother’s engagement dress. So there were two layers of memory here in some way. I would have never known these areas if she hadn’t taken me there.”

The same woman later took her to another site and told her, ‘I’m part of the land. The land is part of me. I want to be photographed naked in it’. “I’m so honoured that they would trust me to do things like that,” says Matar.

This trust is evident in the work itself, in the 135 portraits that make up Where Do I Go?, an accumulated act of women – including Matar herself – inscribing themselves back into a still-contested landscape. Shot between 2020 and 2025, the monograph was co-published by Beirut’s Kaph Books and the Sidney and Lois Eskenazi Museum of Art last November; in March, full-scale war resumed in Lebanon, with Israeli ground operations in the south. One of the deadliest airstrikes of the conflict occurred in June, just before a ceasefire renewed on 19 June, and on the same day an exhibition of the work in Boston closed. The project was on gallery walls throughout.

When I ask Matar whether work published by a Western-distributed press, and destined for those gallery walls, risks becoming the kind of consumable Middle Eastern grief Western audiences have long had an appetite for. She doesn’t hesitate in her reply. “I completely am aware of a Western audience. But that’s exactly why I don’t want to include this,” she says, referring to straightforward images of destruction. Matar shot those images, and says doing so was important to her, but she deliberately decided to keep them out of the book. 

Such images tell the one truth Western audiences already know how to receive, she reflects – without being altered by it. She once walked out of an exhibition of Arab photographers, she says, because it was “all about the hijab and wars, catered to an American audience the way they want to see it”. 

What might seem like the most predictable question an interviewer can ask a photographer is crucial in this case – what do you hope someone will feel, looking at this in 30 years? “They might just look at it and say, ‘Here we are again’,” Matar laughs, burdened by the dark humour, by the idea that hope might be a luxury she can’t afford. “I’m hoping people would look at it like, ‘Oh my God, look how far we’ve come’.” 

Matar’s book has now been out for months, and will be republished in time for this year’s Paris Photo in November. The war continues to hang like a pendulum, casting its arc over everything beneath it. In the shadow, the question she found on a crumbling wall remains urgent: Where do I go?

items.title: Sergio Valenzuela-Escobedo deconstructs the genealogy of the camera in Mänk’áčen

items.content:
Untitled (Black Sheet), 2017 © Sergio Valenzuela Escobedo, courtesy the artist

Sergio Valenzuela-Escobedo’s latest exhibition, Mänk’áčen (Revision 6), at Mumbai’s Dilip Piramal Art Gallery, National Centre for the Performing Arts, expands on long-term research into the genealogies of the camera in relation to pre-photographic modes of visuality

It all began with the phrase ‘Toumayacha Alakana’, which Sergio Valenzuela-Escobedo encountered during a personal visit to the Yagan Usi Museum in southern Chile. It is attributed to the Fuegians of southern Chile and Argentina and understood to mean “to look with a veiled head”, the artist explains; while considering this a poetic proposition, he became intrigued by its paradoxical nature. “Why must we cover our face to look at the other?” he asks. 

His research led him to the astronomical and scientific expeditions of the 19th century, which brought the camera to Tierra del Fuego for the first time. Valenzuela-Escobedo focused on the French Scientific Mission to Cape Horn in 1882-1883, which sought to photograph the transit of Venus across the Sun. “At first, the box didn’t produce images,” he explains. “Progressively, the camera began to capture images, however, the first people to be photographed [with it] never saw their own image. They simply saw an operator under a cloth looking at them for six to eight minutes.”

For the artist, this encounter can be understood through ‘Toumayacha Alakana’, a Western interpretation that tells us more about the observers’ perception than about how the Selk’nam understood and experienced those first encounters with photography. Struck and intrigued by this colonial projection, he set out to find similar amer/indian expressions used to define the relationship between protophotography and these communities.

“…the first people to be photographed [with it] never saw their own image. They simply saw an operator under a cloth looking at them“

Valenzuela-Escobedo draws on the theories of Czech-Brazilian Vilém Flusser, particularly his conception of the camera as a black box – a technological development performing according to a programme that photographers rarely question. They know how to operate the apparatus, but do not understand the blackness inside the camera. Valenzuela-Escobedo develops this idea by interweaving the camera’s mechanical functioning with notions of belief, cosmologies and what lies beyond human comprehension, and conceptualises it as a form of “mystical mechanics”. 

In considering photographic records of early 19th-century exploratory missions, he positions himself alongside the amer/indian communities depicted in the photographs; both look at the camera, shifting the focus from the subject to the apparatus. “To establish a critical position as a researcher, I chose to become a witness to the relationship between the camera and the Indigenous, rather than reproducing the exoticising tradition of looking at the Other,” he explains. “My interest was in the photographic act itself: the moment in which both the Indigenous person and I encounter and look toward the camera. I centre my research on deconstructing its genesis.” In doing so, Valenzuela-Escobedo expands Flusser’s call to examine the camera as a programmed apparatus by also interrogating its historical and colonial formation.

The artist goes one step further by juxtaposing the early uses of the technological apparatus with the colonial construction of the figure of the ‘savage’ in relation to amer/indian groups. He finds it significant that the arrival of the camera produced an encounter between ‘modern’ and Indigenous technologies of visuality and, even though neither side fully understood the other’s technological and visual systems, it was the Indigenous communities who were positioned as ‘savage’. They became a canvas onto which European observers projected their own anxieties and suspicions about the new technology, he argues, including the belief that the camera could steal the soul. “The fear of photography emerges early within 19th-century European culture itself, when the new photographic device was perceived as a threat,” says Valenzuela-Escobedo.

He mentions Charles Baudelaire, who, in his essay Le Public moderne et la photographie (1859), argued that the camera threatened human imagination by mechanically copying the world. Valenzuela-Escobedo also refers to Théophile Gautier, who suggested that photography was able to capture not only the physical form of a person but also a part of their inner self, rendering the soul visible in the photographic image. Even Roland Barthes described the photographic moment as a form of symbolic death, as the photographed subject becomes an object.

These theories allow Valenzuela-Escobedo to dismantle the longstanding assumption in anthropology and visual culture that Indigenous communities resist being photographed; it also enables him to argue that the projection of European anxieties onto these groups was instrumental in producing the symbolic and monetary value of the photographs. He says: “The explorers would return to Europe with their photographs as trophies, saying: ‘Look, these people refuse to be photographed because they believe that the camera can steal their souls. And yet, look at what I have brought back. Despite their resistance, I managed to capture their image.” The figure of the ‘savage’ Indigenous subject became a staple in Western anthropology, constructed in opposition to the figure of the audacious and heroic European explorer.

The use of the diagram as a conceptual framework and visual form is central to Valenzuela-Escobedo’s research. Its plasticity allows him to construct non-linear narratives which foreground the relational interconnectedness of the different elements constituting his work Mänk’áčen. He explains: “It is important to remember that, although many people perceive diagrams as static, they are constantly in motion because it seeks to explain a system and how it functions.” Mänk’áčen’s diagram is organic; it moves, changes, and takes new shape as the project evolves and different actors become involved. This emphasis on collaboration constitutes another central pillar of Valenzuela-Escobedo’s practice.

From the outset of his research, the artist collaborated closely with the Lafkenche Mapuche community in Puerto Saavedra, Chile in 2017. He deliberately chose not to bring a camera, despite its centrality to his investigation, instead spending time with the community, actively listening and learning about their technologies of visuality. He also participated in spiritual ceremonies through which he witnessed these technologies in practice, such as the nguillatún, a four-day celebration in which the machi (shaman) enters a trance to receive visions indicating what the community must do to secure a stable and harmonious future.

As Mänk’áčen evolves and finds new avenues for dissemination, Valenzuela-Escobedo establishes new collaborations that further develop the project by interweaving local histories of encounters between the camera and ancestral technologies of visuality. He explains: “Through invitations, I collaborate with other researchers who share their findings and significant anecdotes about what has been happening in each place. This gives rise to new tensions within the project.”

In its current iteration at Mumbai’s Dilip Piramal Art Gallery, National Centre for the Performing Arts, the project is concerned with how photographic archives are saved, produced, and maintained, particularly on networked digital platforms, while also addressing how the state’s selective preservation, suppression, or rewriting of historical narratives can contribute to the erasure of history. For the occasion, a new free newsprint publication, Images in Spite of Ourselves by Justo Pastor Mellado, was published by doubledummy, the platform Valenzuela-Escobedo co-founded. 

“No one knows what is going to happen to our stories on Instagram or to each post uploaded to these platforms,” he says. “I study pre-photography, what could be considered cameras or proto-cameras in ancestral cultures. But it is also important to think about where we are headed.”

These nuanced histories of photography are particularly relevant at a time when France prepares to celebrate the bicentenary of photography’s invention, according to the official historical narrative. Valenzuela-Escobedo explains: “From the perspective of the prehistory of the camera and of pre-photography, the camera has extremely ancient origins that have nothing to do with the French or even European version.” The artist reminds us of the Nimrud lens, an eighth-century BCE concave lens made of ground rock crystal, discovered in present-day Iraq and now housed at the British Museum. Although its original function remains uncertain, Valenzuela-Escobedo argues it may have served as one of the earliest optical devices, becoming a breakthrough in the history of visual technologies.

He also draws attention to Hercule Florence’s experiments in Brazil, in which he succeeded in permanently fixing images produced by the camera obscura using silver nitrate on paper. Although Florence’s notebooks show the first known written use of the term ‘photographie’, dating to 1833 – years before it was widely adopted in Europe – his contributions to the history of photography remain largely overlooked. 

Valenzuela-Escobedo turns to artistic speculation to recover and make space for broader histories of photography and their origins. Drawing from the digital records of Imperial museums which are publicly and freely accessible, and juxtaposing them with seemingly unrelated photographs, images and other objects, the artist unsettles the museums’ authority to produce and legitimise knowledge about the objects in their collections, resonating with Ariella Azoulay’s call to intervene in the imperial grammar of photographic archives.

Ultimately, Mänk’áčen is Valenzuela-Escobedo’s attempt to bring a (multi)perspectival approach to the history of the camera and photography. Drawing on Eduardo Viveiros de Castro’s concept of perspectivism, he imagines “an ideal relationship to the medium that is perspectivist, and offers multiplicity, relationality and alterity”. The project situates Indigenous perspectives within the established history of photography, while proposing a shift in how the different histories of photography are unveiled from beneath the black cloth.

Mänk’áčen (Revision 6) by Sergio Valenzuela-Escobedo is on show until 20 September at Dilip Piramal Art Gallery, National Centre for the Performing Arts, Mumbai www.ncpamumbai.com/venue/piramal-art-gallery https://doubledummystudio.com

items.title: In the Studio with Louis Porter
items.excerpt: Louis Porter photographed at The London Library for British Journal of Photography, 25 February 2026. All images © Alice Zoo A member of The London Library for the last decade, Louis Porter uses its historic collection as a means to consider the present day In 1840, eminent V
items.content:
Louis Porter photographed at The London Library for British Journal of Photography, 25 February 2026. All images © Alice Zoo

A member of The London Library for the last decade, Louis Porter uses its historic collection as a means to consider the present day

In 1840, eminent Victorian and man-of-letters Thomas Carlyle called for a new kind of library in Britain. Combining the excellence of the British Museum Library with the option to take books home, this library would give all classes access to knowledge, he argued, adding that “a collection of good books contained all the nobleness and wisdom of the world before us”. The London Library was founded the following year, and moved into the central St James’s Square in 1845. The library remains in the square today, a sprawling network of buildings housing convivial reading rooms, scholarly studies, and shelf after shelf of books. It holds more than one million publications in fact, nearly all of which can be borrowed by members.

The library’s collection dates from the 16th century to the present day, and is considered particularly strong in literature, art, architecture, philosophy, topography and travel; unusually, members are able to browse the bookstacks storing these publications, rather than requesting specific titles be brought to them. This and The London Library’s idiosyncratic classification system – thematic, in alphabetical order – means disparate publications sit side-by-side, and allows for pleasing chance discoveries and curious finds. “I was in on Saturday looking for a book, and next to it found a history of filing cabinets!” chuckles Louis Porter, artist and London Library member. “Of course I brought it home.” 

Porter joined the library a decade ago, pulled in by its gravitational force soon after moving to London. He grew up in the UK but lived in Australia for 13 years, where he started an MFA in photography; on returning to England, he still had his thesis to write, and was in need of a quiet place to work. Stumbling on The London Library he initially questioned paying the membership fee, then reasoned it was a good deal. “I was doing well in Australia, I had a studio and that was very nice, but when I got to London, I soon realised how expensive it is,” he explains. “A desk space in London is as much as a large studio in Australia, so I thought, ‘There’s no way I’m going to have a studio’. 

“Then it occurred to me that, while it’s expensive to pay for a library, if I thought of the library as my studio, I had an incredibly cheap space with nearly unlimited resources. And I could borrow the books! My favourite place to read is lying on the couch, so that was a game-changer.”

“I’m constantly looking for ways to bring groups of images together from different methodologies, from something more instinctual. When you have a very large number of images, you naturally are going to apply some sort of understanding that is unconscious”

Writing the thesis was what brought Porter into the library, but it is not what made him stay. That was down to the millions of photographs in the library’s books, because he has been working with found photography for years. He started out as an image-maker, shooting looping, oblique street photography such as the series Unknown Land in Melbourne or I Love China on an Australia-China Council residency at Red Gate Gallery, Beijing. But he became an “abstract archivist” initially by accident, after a friend had rescued a newspaper’s picture library, otherwise going to be skipped. Feeling compelled to save the photographs, Porter bought the lot then started to work with them, refinding the shot locations and reframing the same scenes. Collapsing the time between the frozen past and the present, this project also subverted the question of authorship. 

He has since rehomed many other unloved collections of images, and often uses them to create funny, thought-provoking publications. The Anatomy of Business (2012) drills into photographs from a financial magazine, isolating gestures, body language and the occasional still life to consider how commerce is embodied; A Catalogue of a Young Country Ladies Library (2023) – a collaboration with Mana Pinto and his gallery, Chiquita Room – showcases early postcards of female readers, and questions the formation of libraries and cultural identities. Desenho (2023) was made with Pedro Torres using images from a drawing course, sold in instalments in Brazil in the 1980s and 1990s; focusing on errors and inconsistencies, it picks at what it means to be directed to make art.

Porter’s practice has also included projects with mail order catalogues, front pages and newspaper microfilm archives; everyday items that on closer examination reveal deeper social structures. “Over the years I’ve collected and saved archives in many different forms,” Porter explains. “And these things started to creep in [to his work]… But it was an important transition, saying what if I stop worrying about trying to project myself as this creative and just rearrange the images already out there? I started thinking about words, that we don’t reference words back to the person who initially coined them but we can use them to do miraculous things. And I’ve been excited about that idea ever since.”

Other projects revolve around more formal archives, though they tend towards the esoteric and even occult. Porter is currently researching a new project in The Warburg Institute, which has a library of 35,000 books on art and science and their relationship with superstition, magic and folk beliefs. He has also worked in The College of Psychic Studies, which includes books on psychology – and parapsychology – collected by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, author of Sherlock Holmes mysteries (and BJP articles). Porter has found many interesting collections in London, off the beaten track but holding the first books printed in English, or early medical manuals, or grimoires (collections of magic spells). An autodidact with an innate love of learning, Porter can spend hours with these tomes. “Images and ideas are my big interest in life,” he shrugs. “I’m not interested in sport or cars.”

The London Library has become a home from home, and Porter is usually there at least twice a week; he will often have about 10 of its books in his actual home too, to read and to photograph. His take on the images in these publications often centres on how they are circulated or understood and, while Carlyle might have described a collection of good books as containing “all the nobleness and wisdom of the world”, Porter’s interventions worry at what might make a ‘good’ book or collection, and what ‘wisdom’ we might glean from them. His 2024 publication Monuments Égyptiens reproduces a 1902 book by Jean Capart, for example; in the original each photographic plate is covered by a thin sheet of tissue, which the viewer can lift, but in Porter’s version the sheet always remains. The images are visible but veiled, he says, just as photographs bring proximity yet also distance.

Monuments Égyptiens was inspired by Porter’s travels through the bookstacks in The London Library, which include many 19th and early 20th century books with such papers; as we journey through the shelves he pulls out an example to show me, a publication featuring delicate insects drawn on the tissue paper, which readers can superimpose – or not – on an image of a hedgerow. The stacks are quiet and hushed; Porter and I spend a morning there without seeing anyone. Spread between different buildings, the library is also labyrinthine – and vertiginous, because some of the flooring in the stacks is made of glass, or metal grids. It is possible to look three storeys down at seemingly endless shelves and books.

Of course the library is not infinite, and neither is human knowledge, and these limitations interest Porter. Physically experiencing the books is important, he says, suggesting knowledge as an embodied, subjective experience rather than strictly objective or rational. When he selects books and images he does so intuitively, he adds, partly relying on unconscious pattern recognition and his emotional reactions; he created his 2025 publication Search Engine – and the 2022 installation that preceded it – over 10 years, after looking at about 60,000 London Library books. The selected images are in the same order as on the shelves, but other forces helped guide what he chose. 

Search Engine plays with the format of index cards, the analogue way to interrogate collections; in both versions of the project the reader flips through images as if flipping through index cards. The result is mysterious, intriguing, baffling; it is an archaeology of evidence, but, without a wider context, extracting meaning becomes hard. Like Larry Sultan and Mike Mandel’s Evidence, Search Engine suggests that evidentiary images only prove what we already think, and it also adds a layer around how we structure and access information. And, with a title referencing contemporary image searches and databases, it also suggests that both digital and analogue archives do the same thing. 

“I‘m interested in the systems that carry images, their conceptual and technical qualities,” Porter says. “When we talk about the logging, the searching through, these are images that are massing in place, images that will relate to other images. So I’m constantly looking for ways to bring groups of images together from different methodologies, from something more instinctual. When you have a very large number of images, you naturally are going to apply some sort of understanding that is unconscious. The feeling of going through these things is almost meditative, and you can apply that to the feeling of scrolling through social media too. Entering into that is, for me, really important.”

Porter approached taking photographs in a similar way, getting a train out of town on the hottest days in Australia then walking home, waiting until he was exhausted – “near delirious” – before starting to shoot. Our current tech-heavy society is an evolution or acceleration of Victorian empiricism, he argues, but there are other ways to engage with the world. “There’s nothing more rational-positivist than the AI systems we’re putting in place,” he reflects. “But somehow something’s creeping around the sides of that – an irrationality, a reassertion of a strange, dark, dreaming space. We’re living in a peculiar time, we’re suspended between a rationalist ideal that wants an ordered world, and a chaotic other.”

He has explored this dichotomy in other projects too. His 2015 publication Optics gathered illustrations from The London Library’s early photographic manuals and treatises, to consider how new forms of looking materialised. One spread of his publication contrasts an image of the interior of the eye with a shot of the surface of the moon, showing new abilities to zoom in very close or very far away, to see far beyond the limits of the human body. Other spreads reproduce diagrams on the movement of light, redrawing the complexity of the world as directions, angles and planes. These diagrams generalise and abstract – they are useful but, as with AI, are also subjective, dependent on what is fed in and how it is analysed. 

Another portfolio, On the Use of Novel Devices from the Distant West (2015), was made on residency in the Awagami paper factory in Japan, and takes its name from the first Japanese publication to describe photography (Ensei Kiki Jutsu, 1854). In it, Porter uses early photographic processes to depict objects from local schools, educational devices such as fossil specimens or engine cross-sections, which he compares to didactic museum objects. A certain way of seeing the world was being invented, disseminated and even imposed – a way of seeing that is now almost second nature. Porter developed his calotypes, cyanotypes and salt prints with local eggs, milk, salt and potato starch, and with paper produced in the factory. It produces both supple, more translucent Japanese sheets and stiffer, more opaque Western types. 

Porter’s The Appearance of Distance (2024), which was exhibited in Paris Photo’s 2025 Emergence sector, considers how we perceive range and space; including diagrams, found images of hands and faces, and wooden sticks measuring acceptable social distances in various cultures, it ponders the shift from interpreting the world via one’s own body to measuring in abstract terms. The series is named after Walter Benjamin’s description of aura, a specificity of things he believed was being lost with modernity; the accompanying text is by Esther Leslie, professor of political aesthetics at Birkbeck, University of London, and highlights Benjamin’s reference to the “wilfully subversive protest against the typical, classifiable”, his efforts “to banish Newton’s mechanistic, mathematical Enlightenment physics”. “Adorno speaks of a Cartesian ambition, in which ‘items of knowledge’ are ‘pinned down and identified like things – photographable’,” Leslie writes. “But what is a photograph actually?”

It is a problem Porter also poses. Photographs are slippery, he says, they tell us more about us than the world; they are “a very quick, intuitive way to observe the absurdity of our condition”. Like Leslie, he questions whether we have understood photographs, let alone digital or post-digital images. For him, it is another good reason to consider The London Library his study or studio. “Slightly older archives are conceptual windows to view now,” he says. “I always think that, if you want to observe the present, it’s better to look at what you’ve just passed. In the same way, I like to sit with my back to the direction of travel.

“We’re in a technological revolution, and the last time we had a moment like that was the Industrial Revolution. And you know, for the Victorians reality became very porous. They started to get interested in science fiction, in the occult, in escaping the earthly realm with technology, and that’s happening to us too. There’s a tendency to think of our age as a repetition of the build-up to World War Two, but I don’t know. I think we’re Victorians again.”

items.content:
Window of Hill’s Gents Tailoring. Covent Garden, London. October 22, 1986 © Jim Dow

A new exhibition drawing on the Martin Parr Foundation’s collection reveals an eerie weird in the everyday 

It’s not altogether clear what you’re looking at. There’s cosy familiarity in the curling typeface of the Boots logo, but the charred walls, upturned cupboard and exposed metal bones of the blackened building suggest a different story. The aftermath of something terrifying? Knowing that Sarah Pickering’s 2008 series Incident depicts simulated environments used by the fire service for training only enhances the eeriness. This is a documentation of fiction, the remnants of a nightmare rehearsed. 

Pickering’s work will be on display in Dark Tales, a forthcoming show at Martin Parr Foundation (MPF) that digs into the MPF’s 5000-strong print collection to consider documentary photography’s gothic tendencies. Horror is the mood of the moment. Wild fires rage, AI chatbots take our jobs and a Frankenstein remake streams on Netflix. The birth of Gothic fiction in the 18th century – which delivered both Frankenstein and Dracula – coincided with the dawn of the Industrial Revolution; then as now, accelerated technological progress, medical advances and rapid urbanisation were changing life, work and what it meant to be a human. 

“None of these photographers would necessarily deem their work gothic,” curator Isaac Blease explains. “We’re using the gothic as a window to look at these works in a different context and see what meanings can be evoked.” Blease curated another exhibition from the MPF’s collection two years back, ONE YEAR! Photographs from the miners’ strike 1984 – 85, but where ONE YEAR explored what photographs can do, pragmatically –  “how they were used as part of that resistance movement, but also used by the media to skew perceptions of the miners” – this time, Blease is looking at how photographs can make us feel.

“[Darkroom processing is] inherently gothic in the way that it memorialises.” Isaac Blease, curator, Martin Parr Foundation

Adopting motifs from the Gothic literary tradition, the exhibition is divided into chapters, with a deliberately disrupted chronology. ‘The Castle’ sets the scene portraying “The land as a repository for things that happened in the past,” as Blease puts it. Bill Brandt and Lee Miller present a postwar Britain of rubble and smog, where the ghosts of the conflict still dwell. The mid-20th century marks a turning point, says Blease, in which “photographers weren’t just working under commission or purely as historical record makers, they also had their own subjective visions”. Janine Weidel’s extraordinary images of 1970s Stoke-on-Trent iron and steelworks help illustrate what he means; heavy industrial machinery looms like a mythical monster above diminutive human figures. 

‘Domestic Bliss’ centres on the home, a place where repressed emotions resurface in unexpected ways. Anna Fox’s beautiful still lifes of increasingly bizarre dishes, fashioned for her by a Falklands veteran houseguest, manifest a PTSD in which trauma transforms the everyday into something incomprehensible. In disturbing the mundane, “the gothic can be playful as well as being dark,” Blease adds, and Martin Parr’s image of twee suburban Conservative supporters shows what he means; they people depicted are simply gathering in a garden but, shot from behind some low shrubbery, the frame suggests a ludicrous menace. Similarly, Jo Spence’s stark image of a disembodied foot has the sinister feel of a crime scene, but contains her characteristic undercurrent of wry humour.

Chris Shaw’s photographs of his time as a hotel night porter appear in ‘Night Creatures’. The pictures, shot in the 1990s, touch on questions of labour, working in poorly-paid jobs on zero hour contracts, and an intense nighttime world; they are also “evocative in the blurring and overburning of the flash,” says Blease. Stretched out on a satin couch, Jordi the Lounge Lizard suggests a cadaver in an open casket in this context, the photographs lent new meaning in their interactions. 

In ‘Double Take’, the chapter featuring Pickering’s Boots, things are never quite what they seem. The suits in Jim Dow’s image of an old-school Covent Garden tailors – anachronistic even in 1986 – seem to float, phantom-like. A bed with crisp white, neatly folded sheets and a floral curtain turns out to be a cell from the notorious Northern Irish Maze prison. Photographed by Donovan Wylie, this vision of a now-sanitised site of violence and incarceration makes us consider how troubling histories can seem to lodge in physical objects and spaces.

Blease believes photography is susceptible to this effect, given that it contains a ghostly trace of what was; darkroom processing chemistry is almost magical, alchemical, “inherently gothic in the way that it memorialises,” he asserts. “Things that are in the image are no longer there in reality afterwards.” The earliest subjects feared the camera would steal their souls, and photography was first popularised by spiritualists and showmen – who were attempting to prove the presence of otherworldly creatures, or to deliberately mislead. 

The show’s title refers to documentary photography, acknowledging the genre that dominates the MPF collection but also complicating the idea of documentary as photographic realism. The selected images portray ‘real’ aspects of Britain but, in looking awry, reveal a hitherto unnoticed strangeness in them. Curating the show was an intense process which took Blease a year and a half, initially selecting images instinctively then as they related to his research in the Gothic literary tradition. In the last stretch, “it became much more about a kind of conjuring of atmosphere, metaphor or suggestion,” Blease explains, though that’s an explanation that remains enigmatic, because it’s hard to pinpoint what gives an image a haunted quality. 

What is it about the otherwise average double bed in John Myers’ photograph that makes the bulging pillows look threatening? Perhaps the secret is in the mystery. Creative writers are told to ‘show, don’t tell’, and the photographs here do something similar, lingering in uncertainty. We tend to discuss photography in terms of light but the shadows have always been there, and they are always just as important.

Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic runs from 17 September to 20 December 2026 at Martin Parr Foundation, Bristol martinparrfoundation.org Dark Tales is part of the 2026 Bristol Photo Festival, more information on the full programme can be found at bristolphotofestival.org

items.title: The right not to be perceived: structural refusal, false prophets, and the decolonial frame
items.excerpt: New British Views #21, England, 2022 © Marwan Bassiouni In Partnership with Soul City Arts & University of Warwick For decades, Muslim artists have been told that representation is progress. Ahead of the Good Muslim/Bad Muslim symposium, the photographers
items.content:
New British Views #21, England, 2022 © Marwan Bassiouni

In Partnership with Soul City Arts & University of Warwick

For decades, Muslim artists have been told that representation is progress. Ahead of the Good Muslim/Bad Muslim symposium, the photographers and researchers reshaping the visual arts are making the case for something more radical: the right not to be perceived.

What does it mean to photograph a community that has spent decades being surveilled, ridiculed, and filtered through neo-Orientalist structures? For Muslim lens-based artists, visibility in the West has long carried an excessive price: the enforcement of a “sanitized Muslim” trope that demands both perfection and submission at the expense of complexity.

In 1978, long before the pivotal aftermath of 9/11, Palestinian scholar Edward Said wrote in Covering Islam: How The Media and the Experts Determine How We See The Rest of The World that it had become part and parcel to deliberately distill the actually wildly dynamic Muslim socio-political and cultural world – a vibrant tapestry spanning dozens of countries, cultures, and ethnicities – as a region and a people of a “timeless childhood, shielded from true development by an archaic set of superstitions, prevented by its strange priests and scribes from moving out of the Middle Ages into the modern world.”

Nearly half a century later little has fundamentally changed when it comes to how Muslims are portrayed and perceived in the West. The “sanitized Muslim” trope still mandates that Muslim identity must be palatable, quiet, and “perfect” – a tendency which was recently painstakingly dissected in Mohammed El Kurd’s Perfect Victims – to gain societal acceptance, placing a heavy psychological burden on individuals. The image is curated to soften, and any shred of complexity is lost in a sea of commodification, with the ultimate goal being to entertain rather than to meaningfully involve the audience by making them question their role in what they are observing.

Simultaneously, the colonial convention of putting others on display as if they were mere curiosities remains ubiquitous, leaving little room for the authentic, complex, and complicated Muslim experience.

To challenge these suffocating conditions in the visual arts, Soul City Arts and the University of Warwick have partnered to stage The Good Muslim, Bad Muslim photography symposium. Driven by artistic director Mohammed Ali Aerosol and academic lead Dr. James Hodkinson, and curated by Mohamed Somji, the event serves as a critical, collaborative effort to interrogate these media pressures and explore the visual arts as a space for defiance and authentic self-expression.

Described by academic Dr. James Hodkinson as an “intervention” to “disrupt, rework, and refresh” the status quo, the symposium aims to answer pertinent questions: how do our media, our politics, our arts sector, its policies, even our visual culture itself, continue to influence how Muslims see themselves and show themselves in their art? Have our visual vocabularies become limited?”

In an attempt to answer these questions – or at the very least, rigorously debate them – the Good Muslim, Bad Muslim symposium offers a dynamic line-up of speakers. In his opening keynote, independent photographer and writer Asim Rafiqui will interrogate the figure of the “good Muslim” as constructed by Western media and photojournalism: the “integrated” apolitical subject whose visibility depends on silence about empire, occupation, and the imperial geographies from which diasporic Muslim communities so often emerge.

“When such magazines give attention to you, you feel like you have arrived. It’s a very seductive and drunken place to be.”

©Asim Rafiqui
©Asim Rafiqui

Tripping over the Line

Rafiqui still remembers the exact moment he realized he had to quit his job and radically change not only the world he navigated professionally but the world at large. In the aftermath of 9/11, Rafiqui was regularly traveling the world on assignment for many of the world’s leading legacy publications. His career was on a fast upward trajectory, fueled by what he saw as a genuine appreciation of his craft.

“When such magazines give attention to you, you feel like you have arrived,” he recalls. “It’s a very seductive and drunken place to be. You stop thinking. You simply start chasing and trying to stay in the mix.”

Then, in 2006, Rafiqui stopped by a New York magazine office to pitch a personal project on Evangelical Christianity in America—a stark departure from the ‘war and terrorism’ stories he was routinely dispatched to cover in Pakistan. The editor’s response was a brusque reality check: “Well, why would I call you for any work in America? You have no competitive advantage.”

Despite having lived in the U.S. for nearly twenty years, Rafiqui was being systemically pigeonholed. “A wall had collapsed,” he says. “I was actually chosen because I was this convenient portal to what they considered to be some bizarre culture they thought I would have secret access to … the Taliban whisperer, if you like. Outside of that, they couldn’t fathom how they would possibly ever use me.” Later, a friendly deputy editor pulled him aside with a warning: “Listen, Asim, If you want to be the photographer you want to be, you will have to do it all on your own.”

It proved to be a critical juncture. After “tripping over the line”, Rafiqui walked away from the imperial terror fantasies, refusing to allow legacy institutions to impose a fixed identity on him. “You realize that you were only in the mix because you were as racist, as essentialist, as derogatory as they were,” he reflects. “It wasn’t like you were doing anything new or changing anything. You were just feeding the machine.”

For Rafiqui, the post-October 7 critical juncture completely shattered any remaining illusions pertaining to mainstream moral progress. “Obviously these last few years have shown us clearly what we’re dealing with. And if we don’t wake up now, after everything that we’ve literally seen, then either we’re dead inside or … it’s our own fault to not regroup and change how we’re doing things. If we’re working in exactly the same way as we were before October 2023, then there’s something fundamentally wrong.”

New British Views #12-1, England, 2021 © Marwan Bassiouni

Digital Absence as an Act of Preservation

After a career in photojournalism left her with a profound sense of unease and dissatisfaction with the industry, visual researcher Shaista Chishty – a former student of Rafiqui who will present her paper The Case for Opacity: A Radical Alternative to Performing the Good Muslim – decided to dissect the visual traps she encountered in her practice-based PhD at Cardiff University. This disillusionment was awakened during her work in humanitarian photojournalism, where she found herself increasingly estranged from the compromised visual culture surrounding the development field.

“The typical get flown out and document whatever’s happening in a country you have probably never been to, know little about, with a focus on returning in minimal time with a set of images an editor already had in mind,” Chishty explains. “I remember coming back from Ethiopia and people saying, “Oh, these children look too happy. The kinds of images that were published ultimately reinscribed existing harmful narratives about negatively racialised people. I felt uncomfortable with the objectification of poverty and the grey area concerning ethics and consent.”

In her early work, Chishty analyzed how the niqab was represented in mainstream discourse, juxtaposing it against how veiled women framed themselves. At the time, Chishty too, was considering the potential of self-representation to shift narratives. However, As she continued to observe her social feeds, she began to notice a trend where the images some Muslim women were sharing online were starkly reminiscent of 19th-century Orientalist studio paintings – fantasies often dreamt up by European men who had never even travelled to the so-called ‘Orient’. “And I thought, why is the aesthetic the same?.. that is what I am seeking to understand through my PhD research.”

Drawing on her work as a photographer and researcher, Chishty’s PHD research argues that visibility is a trap: rather than delivering true recognition and freedom, it exposes Muslims to increased surveillance, scrutiny, and institutional control, ultimately reinforcing the very “good Muslim, bad Muslim” binary it claims to resist. In an era of mandatory digital self-fashioning, she turns to Édouard Glissant’s demand for the right to opacity, the right to be unknown and a refusal of legibility as a radical alternative and political act in the face of Islamophobia. True subversion, Chishty suggests, lies in the strategic breaking with convention and imagining alternatives: regrouping, learning and experimenting in ways which refuse expectations.

To build visual and creative languages entirely on one’s own terms, Chishty says, we need to better understand visual histories, how they live on in the present, and address our own complicity. This non-compliance requires resisting a system built explicitly to isolate and fracture collective power. “The system does try to separate us to make us despair… When we’re together, we’re better. But the system is deliberately designed to make us compete with each other.”

The wider itinerary of the symposium mirrors this deep exhaustion with institutional surveillance, expanding the inquiry into physical and generational landscapes. In New Western Views, Amsterdam-based photographer Marwan Bassiouni offers a quiet, contemplative alternative to the media’s relentless obsession with spectacle by documenting Western landscapes entirely from the interior windows of mosques, framing an understated localized coexistence where Muslim presence is simply woven into the national fabric. While his work comfortingly allows Muslims to merely be, rather than having to prove anything to anyone, it is perhaps made stronger by the juxtaposition with the everyday Islamophobia that runs rampant in Europe in real life.

And where Bassiouni looks out from the sacred interior to zone in on a calmer coexistence, Birmingham-based photographer Mahtab Hussain reverses the lens entirely, confronting the claustrophobic reality of a community under constant, algorithmic surveillance. In What Did You See?, his documentation of Birmingham’s Muslim communities by photographing every mosque in the city, Hussain exposes how the apparatus of counter-terrorism and urban surveillance transforms everyday working-class neighborhoods into open-air panopticons, effectively translating the abstract “Bad Muslim” paradigm into a tangible, lived reality of digital profiling and architectural containment.

Where Hussain’s stark typologies map the claustrophobic outer boundaries of this state-sponsored dystopia, the symposium offers a radical counter-strategy by retreating from the hyper-scrutinized public square into the sacred, domestic interior of the Muslim home. This profound shift from external surveillance to internal sanctuary forms the emotional core of the Thread and Trace panel, where artists Nilupa Yasmin and Miriam Ali, alongside moderator Dr. Fatima Rajina, dismantle the voyeuristic demands of the Western gaze by turning toward the tactile, generational archives of textile and fabric.

By replacing the eerie electronic eye of the police camera with the intimate, restorative acts of handling, unpicking, and reweaving inherited garments and prayer rugs, these artists create a site of creative refusal – one where identity refuses to become a spectacle performed for institutional acceptance but is instead quietly nurtured through a visceral, deeply felt devotion – with the object outliving the person who wore it into meaning.

Likely to be the most intimate part of the symposium, What We Don’t Say is the culmination of a longer process. Ahead of the event, practitioners were invited to submit a short, anonymous reflection on an unresolved tension in their work – a moment they changed or softened their art knowing who might see it. A curated sequence of these testimonies will be read aloud in a closed listening circle, followed by small-group conversations where attendees can sit with disagreement rather than letting a single debate play out across the room. This session runs under strict closed-door terms: no recording, no attribution, and no press. 

This setup will honour the symposium’s argument that the pressures shaping Muslim representation are often deeply internalized long before an institution or audience ever sees the actual output. Ultimately, any person of colour navigating the contemporary art world is keenly aware of the massive emotional toll it takes to perpetually perform for audiences from which nuance is intentionally withheld in spaces that remain shackled to neo-Orientalist structures.

Professor Mahmood Mamdani, the author of Good Muslim, Bad Muslim, will conclude the symposium with a short reflection on some of the the ideas that inspired the symposium.

The Good Muslim/Bad Muslim symposium takes place on Monday, September 7 at Oxford House, Bethnal Green, London

Written by Farah-Silvana Kanaan
